newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FOCUS-Romania fights inflation with monetary levers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Romania fights inflation with monetary levers.

text.p: Romania forged ahead on Thursday with plans to use monetary levers to fight rising inflation, restore confidence in the leu and put the economy and market reforms on track.

Central Bank governor Mugur Isarescu told a news conference tough monetary policy, an austerity budget and structural reforms, would help Romania achieve macro-economic stability and win the support of international lenders.

"This is the first time we are taking the bull by the horns," Isarescu said of a government package announced this week aimed at winning loans of about $1.0 billion from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank.
The pledges appeared to be taking shape.

An auction for refinancing funds sent the average one-week rate soaring to 226.35 percent from last week's 125.45 percent after the central bank severely restricted the amount of funds on offer on a cash-starved money market.
"All my rates will jump accordingly from tomorrow," said a trader with a foreign bank operating in Bucharest.

Romania's new centrist coalition government, which ousted ex-communists in last November's elections, pledged in its programme to cut bulging budget and trade deficits, speed up privatisation and slim down communist-era industries.
Isarescu said the central bank was determined to mop up excess money supply to restore confidence in the leu, which has sunk to about 9,000 per dollar from 4,000 in the New Year.

"We will control money supply through tough control over reserve money, the core of broad money," Isarescu said. Reserve money, also known as high-powered money, includes cash in circulation and in vaults and banks' minimum reserves.
President Emil Constantinescu's coalition pledged in the election to bridge the gap which has left reforms far behind those in ex-communist Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic.

This week's programme emerged from a month of talks with senior IMF officials who complained that the ex-communists who ran Romania after the 1989 execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu had consistently failed to deliver on promises.
The central bank has already started to drain liquidity from the market to create "leu hunger". Short-term money market rates have climbed to 160 percent from 52 in early January.
"The central bank is aiming for those who keep their leu to have substantial gains this year," he said.

Isarescu said money supply growth in the months ahead would be below inflation rates. He said a "blip" of price rises would continue for some months following the freeing of prices for fuel, electicity and food, introduced from this week.
"Monthly inflation will slow in the last quarter of 1997, when we can start a process under which money supply growth will exceed inflation," he said.
Monthly inflation soared to 13.7 percent in January from 10.3 percent last December and is forecast to slow to about 2.2 percent by end-1997.
Isarescu said he hoped the leu's depreciation this year would be lower than inflation, which he estimated at a year-on-year 89.5 percent, compared to 56.9 percent in 1996.

The leu's rate, he said, would be set strictly by market forces after the BNR removed market curbs this week. Licences were issued to 24 banks to act as market makers alongside the only four banks empowered to do so for most of the past year.

Isarescu said that despite some "disorderly moves" in the in the next few days the market would eventually eliminate large gaps between dealers and integrate prices. "It is a war of attrition but it will clearly subside," he said.
